title: Chapter 121 — Midnight.—The Forecastle Bulwarks
paragraphs: Stubb and Flask mounted on them, and passing additional lashings over the anchors hanging there.

"No, Stubb; you can pound that knot there as much as you like, but you'll never pound into me what you were just saying. And how long is it since you said exactly the opposite? Didn't you once say that any ship Ahab sails in ought to pay something extra on its insurance, just as if it were loaded with powder barrels aft and boxes of lucifer matches forward? Hold on, now; didn't you say that?"

"Well, suppose I did? What then? I've partly changed my flesh since that time; why not my mind? Besides, supposing we really are loaded with powder barrels aft and lucifer matches forward — how the devil could the matches catch fire in this drenching spray here? Why, my little man, you have pretty red hair, but you couldn't catch fire now. Shake yourself; you're Aquarius, the Water-bearer, Flask; a man might fill pitchers at your coat collar. Don't you see, then, that for these extra risks the Marine Insurance companies have extra guarantees? Here are hydrants, Flask. But listen again, and I'll answer you the other thing. First take your leg off the crown of the anchor here, though, so I can pass the rope; now listen. What's the mighty difference between holding a mast's lightning-rod in the storm and standing close by a mast that hasn't got any lightning-rod at all in a storm? Don't you see, you timber-head, that no harm can come to the holder of the rod unless the mast is struck first? What are you talking about, then? Not one ship in a hundred carries rods, and Ahab — yes, man, and all of us — were in no more danger then, in my poor opinion, than all the crews in ten thousand ships now sailing the seas. Why, you King-Post, you, I suppose you would have every man in the world go about with a small lightning-rod running up the corner of his hat, like a militia officer's skewered feather, and trailing behind like his sash. Why don't you be sensible, Flask? It's easy to be sensible; why don't you, then? Any man with half an eye can be sensible."
"I don't know that, Stubb. You sometimes find it rather hard."

"Yes, when a fellow's soaked through, it's hard to be sensible, that's a fact. And I'm just about drenched by this spray. Never mind; catch the turn there and pass it. It seems to me we're lashing these anchors down now as if they were never going to be used again. Tying up these two anchors here, Flask, is like tying a man's hands behind his back. And what big, generous hands they are, to be sure. These are your iron fists, eh? And what a grip they have, too! I wonder, Flask, whether the world is anchored anywhere; if she is, though, she swings on an uncommonly long cable. There, hammer that knot down, and we're finished. There; next to setting foot on land, landing on deck is the most satisfying thing. Say, just wring out my jacket tails for me, will you? Thanks. They laugh at long-togs so, Flask; but it seems to me a long-tailed coat ought always to be worn in every storm at sea. The tails, tapering down like that, carry the water off, you see. Same with cocked hats; the cocks make gutters at the gable-ends, Flask. No more monkey-jackets and tarpaulin hats for me; I must climb into a swallow-tail coat and jam on a beaver hat; there. Hallo! Whew! There goes my tarpaulin overboard! Lord, Lord, that the winds that come from heaven should have such bad manners! This is a nasty night, lad."
